extracted.intended_audience: USPTO patent examiners (and patent practitioners reading MPEP guidance)
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for examining patent applications for subject-matter eligibility (35 U.S.C. 101) and utility (35 U.S.C. 101 / 112(a)), including how to support rejections, evaluate applicant responses, and the evidentiary/showing requirements for assertions of well‑understood/routine/conventional elements and utility.

rubrics_metrics.name: Support required to assert additional elements are well-understood, routine, conventional
rubrics_metrics.description: Examiners should not assert that an additional element (or combination of elements) is well-understood, routine, or conventional unless the examiner finds and expressly supports the rejection in writing with one or more of the following.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Allowed supports: (A) A citation to an express statement in the specification or to a statement made by an applicant during prosecution that demonstrates the well-understood, routine, conventional nature of the additional element(s). (The specification demonstrates this when it describes the elements as well-understood/routine/conventional, as commercially available, or in a manner indicating they are sufficiently well-known that the specification need not describe particulars to satisfy 35 U.S.C. 112(a). A finding cannot be based only on silence in the specification.) (B) A citation to one or more of the court decisions discussed in MPEP § 2106.05(d). (C) A citation to a publication that demonstrates the well-understood, routine, conventional nature (e.g., book, manual, review article) showing the elements are widely prevalent or in common use; mere presence in a single patent/publication ordinarily insufficient. (D) A statement that the examiner is taking official notice of the well-understood, routine, conventional nature, used only when certain based on personal knowledge that elements are widely prevalent or in common use; follow procedures in MPEP § 2144.03. Examiners should provide evidentiary support rather than rely on bare assertions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Nature and sufficiency of publication evidence
rubrics_metrics.description: Publication evidence must demonstrate that additional elements are widely prevalent or in common use in the relevant field, comparable to elements so well-known that they need not be described in detail to satisfy 35 U.S.C. 112(a).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: An appropriate publication could include books, manuals, review articles or other sources describing the state of the art and what is well-known and in common use. Whether a document is a 'printed publication' under 35 U.S.C. 102 is distinct from whether it establishes well-understood, routine, conventional activity. A single patent or published application generally will not suffice unless it demonstrates widespread prevalence or common use.

rubrics_metrics.name: Limitations on using official notice
rubrics_metrics.description: Official notice that an element is well-understood/routine/conventional should be used only when the examiner is certain based on personal knowledge that the element is widely prevalent or in common use in the relevant field.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If official notice is taken, examiners must follow procedures for taking official notice and addressing an applicant’s challenge (see MPEP § 2144.03). If applicant challenges such official notice, the examiner must provide one of the evidentiary items (A)-(C) above or an affidavit/declaration under 37 CFR 1.104(d)(2) setting forth specific factual statements and explanation to support the position.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ensure claim limitations match court-found elements and level of generality
rubrics_metrics.description: Examiners should ensure the claim limitations before the examiner are the same as those found to be well-understood, routine, conventional by the courts and recited at the same high level of generality.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: It is not enough that the additional elements are similar to elements at issue in cited cases; they must be recited in the same manner/level of generality. Court decisions discussed in MPEP § 2106.05(d) do not imply that all computer functions are well-understood/routine/conventional, nor that a generic computer component performing a generic computer function is necessarily ineligible. See MPEP § 2106.05(f) and cases such as DDR Holdings for examples where generic components in combination can be 'significantly more.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Form paragraph usage for 35 U.S.C. 101 rejections
rubrics_metrics.description: Prescribed form paragraphs must be used in examining and writing rejections based on 35 U.S.C. 101 and related subject-matter eligibility determinations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use form paragraphs 7.04.01, 7.05, and 7.05.01 for rejections based on failure to claim an invention within statutory categories. Use 7.04.01, 7.05, and 7.05.016 for rejections based on claims directed to a judicial exception without providing an inventive concept/significantly more (Step 2B). If the judicial exception is a 'tentative abstract idea' (does not fall within MPEP § 2106.04(a)(2) groupings), also use 7.05.017 and include the TC Director's signature. Form paragraph 7.04.01 must precede first use of 35 U.S.C. 101 in all first actions and final rejections. Follow local Examiner Notes for ordering and accompanying text.

rubrics_metrics.name: Contents required in form paragraph 7.05.016 (nonstatutory, judicial exception)
rubrics_metrics.description: The rejection must state that the claimed invention is directed to [exception] without significantly more and explain why the exception is not integrated into a practical application and why additional elements do not amount to significantly more.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Bracketed items: [1] identify whether the claim is directed to a law of nature, natural phenomenon (including a product of nature), or an abstract idea; [2] recite what the claims recite as the judicial exception; [3] explain why the judicial exception is not integrated into a practical application; [4] identify additional elements and explain why, separately and in combination, they do not add significantly more (e.g., merely storing/retrieving info in memory are well-understood/routine/conventional computer functions). Include discussion of data gathering as insignificant extra‑solution activity or putting a product of nature into a generic container as nominal/token extra‑solution activity.

rubrics_metrics.name: TC Director approval and contents for form paragraph 7.05.017 (tentative abstract idea)
rubrics_metrics.description: Use 7.05.017 when treating a 'tentative abstract idea' as an abstract idea; TC Director approval and signature are required.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In bracket 1, justify why the claim limitation(s) is/are being treated as an abstract idea even though they do not fall within the groupings in MPEP § 2106.04(a)(2) (e.g., explain why the limitation is among the 'basic tools of scientific and technological work'). In bracket 2, insert the TC Director's signature. Also explain identification of the exception (how it is recited and why it is an exception) and why the combination of additional elements fails to integrate the exception into a practical application.

rubrics_metrics.name: Examiner duties when evaluating applicant’s response to eligibility rejection
rubrics_metrics.description: After identifying reasons why a claim is directed to a judicial exception without significantly more, the burden shifts to the applicant to amend the claim, present persuasive arguments, or submit evidence; examiners must carefully consider all of applicant's arguments and evidence rebutting the rejection.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If applicant amends, determine the amended claim’s broadest reasonable interpretation (BRI) and re-perform the subject-matter eligibility analysis. If applicant's amendment, evidence, or arguments persuasively establish eligibility, the rejection should be withdrawn. If an additional element alone does not integrate the exception, it may still do so in combination with other elements (generic computer components can in combination perform non-generic functions).

rubrics_metrics.name: Appropriate examiner rebuttals and reconsideration triggers when maintaining rejection
rubrics_metrics.description: If applicant properly challenges examiner findings but the examiner deems it appropriate to maintain the rejection, the examiner must provide a rebuttal in the next Office action and may need to provide additional support or explanations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: (1) If applicant challenges a tentative abstract idea based on a court case and not persuasive, explain why the abstract idea is similar to the concept in the cited case. (2) If applicant presents specific argument/evidence that additional elements are not well-understood/routine/conventional, reevaluate and, if maintaining, consider whether evidence should be provided to support the rejection; if official notice was taken and challenged, provide items (A)-(C) or an affidavit/declaration. (3) If applicant adds a generic computer or claims 'specially programmed', look to whether the added elements integrate the exception into a practical application; merely adding a generic computer/programming does not automatically overcome eligibility rejections (see Alice and OIP Techs.). (4) If applicant argues lack of preemption, reconsider Step 2A (improvement to functioning of a computer/technology) and Step 2B (inventive concept in combination).

rubrics_metrics.name: Clarifying the record when claims are found eligible
rubrics_metrics.description: When claims are deemed patent eligible, the examiner may make clarifying remarks on the record to explain the rationale and assist applicant understanding.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Clarifying remarks can reference the portion of the specification describing claimed improvements and note claim elements producing that improvement. Remarks can be made during prosecution or with a notice of allowance. Clarifying explanations (e.g., BRI) are useful to help applicant respond to rejections (example: explain that a computer-readable medium claim's BRI covers a carrier wave and suggest narrowing amendments).

rubrics_metrics.name: Initial steps for utility examination
rubrics_metrics.description: Office personnel must follow procedures when reviewing applications for compliance with the utility requirement: read the claims and supporting written description, determine what applicant has claimed including specific embodiments, and ensure the claims define statutory subject matter.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If at any time it is readily apparent that the claimed invention has a well-established utility, do not impose a rejection based on lack of utility. Ensure claims define a process, machine, manufacture, composition of matter, or improvement thereof.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of a well-established utility
rubrics_metrics.description: An invention has a well-established utility if (i) a person of ordinary skill in the art would immediately appreciate why the invention is useful based on invention characteristics, and (ii) the utility is specific, substantial, and credible.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If a utility is well-established, no rejection for lack of utility should be imposed. The criteria focus on immediate appreciation by a POSITA and the sufficiency (specific/substantial/credible) of the asserted utility.

rubrics_metrics.name: Specific and substantial utility requirement and credibility assessment
rubrics_metrics.description: A claimed invention must have a specific and substantial utility; utilities that are 'throw-away', 'insubstantial', or 'nonspecific' do not satisfy 35 U.S.C. 101.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Credibility is assessed from the perspective of a person of ordinary skill in the art in view of the disclosure and any other evidence of record (e.g., test data, affidavits/declarations, patents, printed publications). An applicant need only provide one credible assertion of specific and substantial utility for each claimed invention to satisfy the requirement.

rubrics_metrics.name: When to reject for lack of utility and concurrent 112(a) rejection
rubrics_metrics.description: If the applicant's asserted specific/substantial utility is not credible, or no assertion is made and there is no readily apparent well-established utility, reject the claims under 35 U.S.C. 101 for lack of utility and under 35 U.S.C. 112(a) (or pre-AIA 112, first paragraph) for failure to teach how to use the invention.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The 112 rejection imposed with a 101 rejection should incorporate by reference the grounds of the corresponding 101 rejection. The examiner should shift the burden to the applicant to (i) explicitly identify a specific and substantial utility and (ii) provide evidence that a POSITA would have recognized that the identified utility was well-established at the time of filing. Ensure adequate nexus between evidence and the properties of the claimed subject matter as disclosed in the application as filed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Requirements for a prima facie showing of no specific/substantial/credible utility
rubrics_metrics.description: A prima facie showing that a claimed utility is not specific/substantial or not credible must establish that it is more likely than not that a POSITA would not consider the asserted utility specific/substantial/credible.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The prima facie showing must contain: (i) an explanation clearly setting forth the reasoning used to conclude the asserted utility is not specific/substantial or credible; (ii) support for factual findings relied upon; and (iii) an evaluation of all relevant evidence of record, including utilities taught in the closest prior art. Where no utility is disclosed or well-established, the showing need only establish that applicant has not asserted a utility and that on the record there is no known well-established utility.

rubrics_metrics.name: Quality of rejection: documentary evidence and scientific explanation
rubrics_metrics.description: Any rejection based on lack of utility should include a detailed explanation and, whenever possible, documentary evidence supporting the prima facie showing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Documentary evidence may include scientific/technical journals, treatise excerpts, books, or patents. If documentary evidence is unavailable, the examiner should specifically explain the scientific basis for factual conclusions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Treatment of applicant factual statements and expert opinions
rubrics_metrics.description: Office personnel must treat as true a statement of fact made by an applicant regarding asserted utility unless countervailing evidence shows a legitimate basis to doubt credibility; accept expert opinions based upon relevant facts whose accuracy is not being questioned.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: It is improper to disregard an applicant's factual statement solely because of disagreement over significance or meaning of the facts. If a prima facie showing of no specific/substantial/credible utility is properly established, application bears burden to rebut via amendment, reasoning, or evidence (e.g., declaration under 37 CFR 1.132, patent, printed publication).

rubrics_metrics.name: Examiner response to applicant rebuttal and withdrawal of rejections
rubrics_metrics.description: If applicant satisfactorily rebuts a prima facie rejection based on lack of utility, the examiner must withdraw the 35 U.S.C. 101 rejection and the corresponding 35 U.S.C. 112 rejection.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When applicant responds, the examiner should review the original disclosure, evidence relied upon in establishing the prima facie showing, any claim amendments, and any new reasoning or evidence. The examiner must recognize, fully consider, and respond to each substantive element of the applicant's response; only where the totality of the record continues to show lack of specific/substantial/credible utility should the rejection be maintained.
